articleSummary: A woman in her 60s with snail contact developed sudden neurocognitive decline and meningitis-like symptoms. After several hospitals, CT scans, and antibiotic therapy with no improvement, she required ICU care. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of cerebrospinal fluid within 24 hours identified the rare parasite Angiostrongylus cantonensis (Guangdong rat lungworm), with exposure likely linked to gardening and snail contact. Targeted therapy led to recovery and discharge. In response to such cases, the Taiwan Society of Infectious Diseases issued guidelines on the clinical use of mNGS for pathogen identification, detailing when to test, specimen collection and transport, testing, and interpretation. mNGS analyzes all nucleic acids against databases for bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, offering critical clues in severe, unclear, or rare infections and when conventional tests fail, while complementing traditional methods. Standardization aims to shorten administrative times and expedite treatment.

articleHeadline: A dose of insecticide killed 97.91% of mosquitoes that spread dengue; a tiny fraction that survived has researchers in Delhi worried
articleSummary: University of Delhi researchers in India report that a laboratory Aedes aegypti strain, the dengue vector, showed 97.91% mortality at the WHO diagnostic dose of α-cypermethrin (10 µg per bottle) in bottle bioassay, slightly below the 98% threshold for susceptibility. In tests with 12 concentrations, four replicates and 20 female mosquitoes per bottle, mortality was recorded at 24 hours. Lakhwani warns this could signal emerging resistance, though survivors were not shown to transmit reduced susceptibility. Biochemical analysis indicated a detoxification enzyme response: β-esterase showed strongest binding to α-cypermethrin, up to ~21-fold at LC50 and ~17-fold at LC90; CYP450 ~2x; α-esterase >7x; glutathione S-transferase declined and acetylcholinesterase showed weak binding. The insecticide targets voltage-gated sodium channels; repeated use may select for resistance traits. Aedes aegypti transmits dengue and spreads Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever. WHO estimates large dengue burden; recommendations include insecticide rotations, biological controls, and household measures to remove breeding sites.

articleSummary: Dengue arrived in Ceará in 1986, imported from Nova Iguaçu, Rio de Janeiro, amid a tourism-driven surge. The first DENV-1 cases appeared in Aracati and later Fortaleza, linked to travelers returning from Rio during an epidemic. The outbreak unfolded as Aedes aegypti, long present in Ceará, enabled sustained transmission; vector reintroductions had been detected in 1984 (Aquiraz) and reinfestation in Fortaleza, with larvae found near BR-116, Mercado São Sebastião, Rodoviário, Port, and Airport. By August 1986, infestation indices in Fortaleza exceeded 30%, and 20 Ceará municipalities were infested, prompting urgent control measures. The Ministry of Health labeled the situation grave. Researchers highlight the vector's adaptability and the health system's limited early responsiveness.
